title: Hanuman's whole personality
hookLine: a mountain carried across the sky, because one herb was needed

lines: A BROTHER WOUNDED. NO TIME TO LOSE.
cards: On a battlefield in Lanka, Lakshmana, Rama's brother, lies wounded, barely breathing. A healer says there is a cure: certain herbs that grow on a mountain far to the north, and they have to be here fast. Hanuman goes.
He crosses the sky, finds the mountain, and then he stops. The herbs are hiding from him, the story says, and he can't tell which ones are needed. There's no time to go back and ask.
So he solves it another way. He lifts the whole peak out of the ground and carries it back through the air, herbs and all. Lakshmana breathes.
Hanuman has a monkey's face, the strength of the wind, and a picture of him hangs in homes and shops. Today's word is why.

teach.h: SEVA — SERVICE, SELF OUT OF THE WAY.
teach.b: Seva. Service. Not service as a job title, and not help with a receipt attached.

Seva is doing what's needed because it's needed, with the self stepped out of the way. Hanuman is the tradition's living picture of it, and notice who he serves: Rama, whom devotees know as God come to earth.
On this path, seva is service offered to God, and done for the people God made. Notice what the mountain story leaves out.

teach.h: NO SPEECH. A MAN BREATHES AGAIN.
teach.b: There's no speech. No moment where he explains how hard it was. The whole story points at one thing: a man on the ground starts breathing again.
The strength is enormous, and it's all aimed outward. The Ramayana does this with him more than once.
When he leaps the ocean and finds Sita in Lanka, what he finally puts in Rama's hand is hers, not his: her jewel, and her message.

Later devotional stories push the picture even further; people tell of him opening his own chest to show that Rama and Sita live inside it. Whatever he has, it's for someone else. And seva doesn't need a mountain.
In temples and homes it's very ordinary work.

teach.h: A FLOOR, A MEAL, A NIGHT'S SLEEP.
teach.b: Washing the floor before the festival. Chopping vegetables for a meal that strangers will eat. Sitting with a sick neighbor so the family can sleep.
Nobody hands out credit for it, and that's part of the point. Because the work is offered to God, the one doing it isn't the hero of the story.
That's why so many homes keep Hanuman's picture: not only for his strength, but for where he aimed it. Hanuman's gifts were huge.

teach.h: WHATEVER HE HAS, IT'S FOR SOMEONE ELSE.
teach.b: The practice works with whatever size yours are.

how: Seva is part of ordinary Hindu life: volunteers clean temples, cook and serve meals at festivals, and care for family and neighbors, and devotees look to Hanuman as the picture of selfless service.

games.q: Nani signed me up for the temple kitchen saturday. SIX hours of onions 😭 she keeps calling it seva. isn't that just free labor??
o: seva is service offered to God, with yourself out of the way. like Hanuman carrying the mountain for Rama.
yeah, it's free labor. skip it if nobody's paying.
it only counts if people see you doing it, so post a pic.
games.why: Hanuman carried a whole mountain so Lakshmana could breathe, and asked nothing back. Seva is service offered to God, with the self out of the way, so Priya's onions are more than chores.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: grow on a mountain to the north
service with the self out of the way

s: Hanuman explains how hard the journey was before handing over the herbs
the story has no speech. it ends with Lakshmana breathing again.
seva can be as ordinary as washing a temple floor
in temples and homes, seva is very ordinary work, done without credit.
seva only counts if someone sees it
seva is offered to God and done because it's needed. nobody hands out credit, and that's part of the point.

games.q: you're Hanuman. you've found the mountain, there's no time to go back and ask, and you can't tell which herbs will save Lakshmana. what do you do?
o: fly back and ask the healer which herb it is.
lift the whole mountain and carry it back.
pick the herb that looks most likely and hope.
games.why: he carries the whole peak through the sky, herbs and all, and Lakshmana breathes. no speech about it, just the need met.

practice: Today's practice: find your herb. Let your shoulders drop. Bring one thing to mind that you're good at.
Staying calm in a mess. Now let one person come to mind who could use exactly that this week. Don't plan it all out.
Just decide: I'll do it, and I won't mention it. Then rest in the decision for the length of the sit. If you pray, you can offer the work before you do it.

wordCard.voice: Seva. Service done because it's needed, with the self out of the way. Hanuman carrying the mountain. Fifteenth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: service, attendance on someone. The same word is used on several paths in India.

carryVoice: Your line: do something for someone, quietly. One small thing today. No post. No mention. Just a mountain moved, and nobody told. Day fifteen.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Hanuman brings the mountain of herbs)
Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Hanuman crosses the ocean and finds Sita)
